content: The incidence of childhood cancers has been increasing over the past two decades, according to the National Cancer Institute. While advancements in medical treatments and technologies have significantly improved survival rates, the long-term effects of cancer and its treatments, particularly those affecting learning and cognitive functions, remain an area requiring further investigation. Research indicates that children with cancer are at an elevated risk of developing various cognitive and learning difficulties. These challenges may arise from direct brain injury caused by the cancer itself, such as brain tumors or metastasis to the central nervous system, or as a result of side effects from cancer treatments like chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Studies have demonstrated that chemotherapy and radiation can damage white matter in the brain and disrupt normal brain activity. Cognitive impairments associated with childhood cancer and its treatments include deficits in attention, working memory, processing speed, mental flexibility, persistence, verbal fluency, memory, motor skills, academic performance, and social functioning. These deficits have been observed regardless of factors such as age, socioeconomic status, time since treatment onset or cessation, anxiety, fatigue, or treatment dosage schedules. To address these cognitive challenges, some clinicians and neuropsychology research groups are developing programs aimed at treating the cognitive impairments linked to childhood cancer. These interventions typically involve cognitive rehabilitation programs designed to either restore impaired cognitive capacities or teach patients strategies to compensate for their impairments. Cognitive rehabilitation generally begins with an evaluation to identify the specific impairments present. This is followed by an individualized program that includes targeted skills training, practice, and the use of metacognitive strategies. Metacognitive strategies focus on enhancing the patient’s self-awareness regarding their problem-solving abilities, teaching them to monitor the effectiveness of these skills, and enabling them to self-correct when necessary. Cognitive rehabilitation is conducted under the supervision of a neuropsychologist or other trained professionals who specialize in this area.
